newsitem.title: FRANCE: Europe's gas industry gears up for era of change.
newsitem.headline: Europe's gas industry gears up for era of change.

text.p: Europe's natural gas industry is on the brink of unprecedented change over the next 15 years, and top gas executives from around the world have been meeting here to debate how it will develop.

The first gas executives summit conference, called by the Institut Francais du Petrol, demonstrated by the number of senior executives who came to address the meeting how seriously the issue is being taken.
Algeria's former energy minister Nordine Ait-Laoussine identified three causes behind 35 years successful growth of the European industry.
He picked out low cost indigenous supplies, abundant further supplies nearby at moderate prices and good relations built up over many years between a small group of participants.
But a number of fundamental changes will require an overhaul in the industry, he added.
"First we will see a change from over-supply in the short-term to a substantial long term deficit as demand rises by up to 50 percent over the next 15 years and supply cannot keep pace.
"Second we will see a change from low cost to high cost imports, as future supply will come from further away at a higher technical cost," Laoussine added.
He said among future sources were talking about such areas as Russia's Yamal peninsula, northern Norway, Algeria, the Barents Sea, Britain's Shetland islands and central Asia.
"Third there is a change from a stable to an unstable market as deregulation undermines the old order," he added. "New buyers and sellers could provide the basis for new volatility."
Pierre Gadonneix, president of Gaz de France, said that the share of natural gas in Europe's energy balance will move from 20 to 25 percent by 2010 or a little later.
He added that security of supply and safeguarding investments abroad will become paramount as the industry grows.

One possible development he foresaw is a change in the nature of contracts as a basic change to the pricing structure of gas, brought about by liberalisation possible development of spot prices means long term contracts may have to exist side by side with new short term deals.

But this view was rejected by Sonatrach director general Nazim Zouioueche, who insisted that producers cannot make investments in a highly capital intensive business if they cannot be guaranteed sales through long term "take or pay" contracts.

Russia's Rem Vyakhirev, chairman of monopoly Gazprom, is central to the future supply question, with gas from the Yamal peninsula in northern Siberia expected to account for much of Europe's needs in the next century. A new pipeline from there will deliver gas to northern Europe, bypassing Ukraine.
This may prove a wise move for Gazprom as supplies bound for Europe now often go missing en route.
"International law is needed to stop Ukraine stealing our gas," he said. "Russia should become more closely involved with the European energy charter."

British Petroleum's chief executive John Browne said gas demand will grow due to a huge abundance of supply, technical change making its use for power generation easier, and political integration in Europe is providing a good regulatory base.
But he feels the biggest driver for change is consumer pressure, as Europe demands a cleaner and more environmentally friendly fuel.
But there were dissenting voices.

The managing director of state utility ENI, Franco Bernabe, pointed out that Italy has already spent between $20 and $40 billion upgrading existing electricity generating plant, and a dash for gas would involve writing this off.
-- Sebastain Alison, Paris newsroom +3314 4197 5050
